summary.text: The speed of light is the speed of electromagnetic waves; in a vacuum it is a universal constant called c, exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.
In a vacuum it is the same for every observer however they move, and it is the upper limit for how fast information, matter or energy can travel.
Light is slower inside materials such as glass or water, and the ratio of c to its speed in a material is called the refractive index.

paragraphs.heading: What the speed of light is
paragraphs.text: The speed of light is simply how fast electromagnetic waves travel. Light is slower inside materials such as glass or water and fastest in a vacuum. That top speed is a universal constant written c, exactly 299792458 metres per second. That works out to roughly a billion kilometres every hour.

paragraphs.heading: Why the number is exact
paragraphs.text: The value is exact because the metre itself is defined by it: by international agreement, a metre is the distance light covers in a vacuum in 1⁄299792458 of a second. The second, in turn, is defined as 9192631770 cycles of radiation from a caesium-133 atom. Before 1983 the metre was defined on its own and the speed of light had to be measured. The fixed value was picked to match the best measurements made before then.

paragraphs.heading: The same for everyone
paragraphs.text: In a vacuum, c is the same for every observer, however fast they move relative to each other. Massless particles and waves, including gravitational waves, travel at c whatever the motion of their source. It is also the upper speed limit for information, matter and energy moving through space. Particles with mass can be pushed ever closer to c but never reach it.

paragraphs.heading: Slower in materials
paragraphs.text: The refractive index n of a material is the ratio of c to the speed v of light inside it, n = c/v. Glass has an index of about 1.5 for visible light, so light in glass moves at roughly 200000 km/s. Air's index is about 1.0003, which leaves light in air only about 90 km/s short of c. Electromagnetic waves along wire cables also move slower than c.

paragraphs.heading: A delay you can notice
paragraphs.text: Over long distances the finite speed of light matters. Much of the starlight we see left its stars long ago, so looking far away lets us study the history of the universe. Signals to distant space probes can take hours to arrive. In computing, the speed of light sets the shortest possible delay for any message, and timing how long light takes to travel lets us measure great distances very precisely.

paragraphs.heading: How we learned it
paragraphs.text: Ole Rømer first showed that light is not instant by watching the apparent motion of Io, a moon of Jupiter. In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell proposed that light is an electromagnetic wave and so moves at c. Albert Einstein took as a starting rule that c is the same in every inertial frame, whatever the source is doing, and built the theory of relativity on it. There c links space and time, and it appears in E = mc².

paragraphs.heading: Why the letter c
paragraphs.text: Nobody is sure why the letter c was chosen. Guesses include c for constant, or the Latin celeritas, meaning swiftness. Maxwell himself used V, and Einstein also used V in his 1905 papers before switching to c in 1907, by which time it had become the standard symbol.
